world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Jany, Carmen. 2009. Chimariko Grammar: Areal and Typological Perspective. UC Publications in Linguistics 142 (eScholarship blocked 403). Dixon 1910 (read on archive.org) has no accent/stress statement.

new_statements.quote: Chimariko shows phonologically predictable stress on the root or the penultimate syllable of the root in polysyllabic roots. [27. ápu ‘fire’; éšoh ‘cold’; šinčéla ‘dog’; mutákweh ‘rain’; mála-ˀi ‘my mother’s sister’] Instances of root stress on the final syllable of polysyllabic roots may occur due to lexicalisation, as in the following example. [28. pʰuncá-lla ‘little girl’; ˀiṭí-lla ‘boy’] Although vowel length is not phonemic, long vowels are found sporadically in the data (see also 2.1.2.3). If a syllable contains a long vowel, it is always stressed.

new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (263 pp., text layer; pdfinfo title "Transcript from Chimariko Sound Recording" is an artefact of the eScholarship deposit, the file is the full UC Press book with front matter, copyright page "(c) 2009 by The Regents of the University of California", UCPL vol. 142) and the. Ran extracted text on PDF pp. 47-48 directly: printed p. 27 heading "2.3 Stress and prosody" / "2.3.1 Stress" then "Chimariko shows phonologically predictable stress on the root or the penultimate syllable of the root in polysyllabic roots." followed by example (27) apu 'fire', esoh 'cold', sincela 'dog', mutakweh 'rain', mala-'i 'my mother's sister' (with accents); p. 28 "Instances of root stress o…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable from morphology: it falls on the root; in polysyllabic roots on the root's penultimate syllable (verb roots, mostly V.CV(C), carry the primary stress; nominal roots carry primary stress on their penultimate syllable, pp. 22-23). Affixes (e.g. y-ečúúda-n, x-ukéé-na-tinda, mála-ˀi) do not attract it. A syllable with a long vowel is always stressed. The only acoustic correlate found is higher pitch (F0), not duration or intensity (p. 28).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Author says primary and secondary stress 'have been marked occasionally in the data' (p. 27) but gives no placement rule for secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Root stress on the final syllable of a polysyllabic root occurs through lexicalisation, e.g. diminutives pʰuncá-lla 'little girl', ˀiṭí-lla 'boy' (p. 28). Long vowels, sporadic and non-phonemic, are always stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (root within the morphological word). Based on archival transcriptions (Harrington, Dixon, Sapir) where stress was only occasionally marked, plus an acoustic analysis of one wordlist recording (Martha Ziegler, recorded by J. P. Marr, 1930s-40s); prosody above the word not describable (2.3.2). Language extinct since the 1930s; no living-speaker verification.
new_statements.identity_note: Chimariko proper (chim1301, ISO cid), extinct c. 1930s. Jany's grammar synthesizes all archival records (Harrington's consultants incl. Sally Noble; Dixon's Friday and Mrs. Dyer; Sapir's 1927 notes) plus one Marr/Ziegler recording; no dialect is singled out for the stress statement. Dixon 1910 notes minor l/r and s/c speaker differences but nothing prosodic.

[27. ápu ‘fire’; éšoh ‘cold’; šinčéla ‘dog’; mutákweh ‘rain’; mála-ˀi ‘my mother’s sister’] Instances of root stress on the final syllable of polysyllabic roots may occur due to lexicalisation, as in the following example. sources.locator: Ch. 2 Phonetics and Phonology, sec. 2.3.1 'Stress', pp. 27-28 (PDF pp. 47-48 of the eScholarship file); supporting: sec. 2.2.2 'Structure of roots', pp. 22-23
sources.note: Sec. 2.3.1 Stress, pp. 27-28: phonologically predictable stress on the root, or the penultimate syllable of the root in polysyllabic roots; final-root-syllable stress only via lexicalisation (diminutives); long vowels always stressed; only acoustic correlate is pitch (higher F0), not duration or intensity; final lengthening. Sec. 2.2.2 pp. 22-23: verb roots carry primary stress; nominal roots carry primary stress on the penultimate syllable. Sec. 2.5 p. 32: neighbours Hupa, Shasta, Wintu are weight-sensitive; Chimariko vowel length on stressed syllables possibly a contact development.
